verified_from: Publisher summary, methods and selected results sections
exposure: Combined 24-hour lighting: brighter daytime exposure and lower night lighting over hospitalization.
finding: Actigraphic sleep duration increased by about 5.9 minutes per hospitalization day; lighting appraisal improved. Subjective sleep, alertness, anxiety and depression did not differ between groups.
limitations: Combined exposure over days does not isolate tone, establish acute calming, or validate device percentages. One participant withdrew with intervention-induced migraine.

study_context.population_setting: 196 cardiology-ward patients; mean age 66.5 ± 13.1 years; median hospitalization 5 days in both study arms.
study_context.design_sample: Controlled clinical trial comparing standard patient-room lighting with an interventional lighting system.
study_context.intervention_exposure: Dynamic 24-hour light/dark cycle with low nocturnal light exposure and 2 hours of bright daytime light at 1750 lux.
study_context.timing_duration: Lighting exposure continued across hospitalization; outcomes were assessed over the admission.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Wrist actigraphy plus questionnaires covering sleep quality, alertness, anxiety, depression and lighting appraisal.
study_context.results_detail: Subjective sleep, alertness, anxiety and depression did not differ between groups. Lighting appraisal was better in intervention rooms for patients (P<0.001) and staff (P<0.005). Actigraphic sleep duration increased by 5.9 min per hospitalization day (95% CI 0.6–11.2; P=0.03); after 5 days the difference was 29 min (7.3%).
study_context.study_limitations_context: The intervention changed the full 24-hour lighting pattern rather than a single isolated lighting component. One participant withdrew because of an intervention-induced migraine.

finding: Differences favoured natural sounds for heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate; mean arterial pressure, perceived stress and oxygen saturation did not differ significantly.
limitations: Mixed outcomes; abstract alone does not establish effects for this individual, a safe dose or absence of adverse effects.

study_context.population_setting: Systematic review and meta-analysis of human studies comparing exposure to natural sounds with a quiet environment.
study_context.design_sample: Systematic review and meta-analysis; the published abstract reports pooled comparisons across several physiological and self-reported stress outcomes.
study_context.intervention_exposure: Natural-sound exposure, including sounds such as birdsong, compared with quiet.
study_context.timing_duration: Exposure timing and duration varied across the included studies.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, mean arterial pressure, perceived stress and oxygen saturation.
study_context.results_detail: Natural sounds differed significantly from quiet for heart rate (P=0.006), blood pressure (P=0.001) and respiratory rate (P=0.032). No significant differences were reported for mean arterial pressure (P=0.407), perceived stress, or SpO2 (P=0.251).
study_context.study_limitations_context: Effects were not consistent across all measured outcomes, and exposure protocols varied across the included literature.

verified_from: Open-access article; selected metric and interpretation sections
study_design: Review of HRV metrics and norms
exposure: Measurement duration, physiological influences and interpretation.
finding: HRV interpretation depends on recording duration and context, including respiration.
limitations: An RMSSD change alone does not establish psychological state or a patient-specific uncertainty interval.

study_context.population_setting: Methodological review covering HRV measurement and norms across healthy and clinical contexts rather than a single patient cohort.
study_context.design_sample: Narrative/methodological review of commonly used time-domain, frequency-domain and nonlinear HRV metrics and their interpretation.
study_context.intervention_exposure: No intervention; the review discusses how HRV values depend on recording duration, physiological mechanisms and measurement context.
study_context.timing_duration: The review distinguishes long-term (~24 h), short-term (~5 min) and ultra-short-term (<5 min) HRV recordings.
study_context.outcomes_measured: HRV metrics including RMSSD, SDNN and frequency-domain measures, with discussion of normative interpretation and recording requirements.
study_context.results_detail: RMSSD is a time-domain measure based on successive normal-to-normal interval differences and is commonly used for short-term HRV. The review emphasizes that HRV interpretation depends on recording duration and physiological context, including respiration.
study_context.study_limitations_context: This is a measurement/interpretation review rather than an intervention trial, and HRV values are sensitive to methodological and physiological context.

finding: Retaining the current brightness is an available choice when compatible with the case. This entry supplies a non-research rationale for that choice. Tone is selected separately within the case restrictions.
limitations: This entry imposes no lighting lock, default preference, veto, or requirement to retain brightness. Other choices may use another applicable basis. A chosen increase/decrease needs its own applicable support; do not cite this retention rationale for those actions. No physiological or sleep benefit is established.

finding: Silence, retaining permissible existing sound, or offering any explicitly preferred allowed sound may respect patient choice. All active sounds remain subject to staff permission and patient prohibitions.
limitations: Preference compatibility is not efficacy evidence. A stated preference does not require playback; explain a decision to retain silence when a permitted preference is supplied.

finding: Report signed current-minus-reference changes; HR/RMSSD percentages use the reference denominator. Report EDA absolute change only. Missing or poor-quality pairs are unavailable.
limitations: These calculations are descriptive. EDA percentage reporting is disabled by design, not because absolute comparisons are invalid.

study_design: Systematic review: 59 articles, 37 music and 22 nonmusic
exposure: Randomized studies of music and nonmusic sound; only one direct comparison.
finding: Reported benefits across pain, sleep and stress/anxiety outcomes; a larger music literature does not establish superiority over nonmusic sound.
limitations: Heterogeneous interventions and outcomes; no fixed AHR playback dose or individual benefit follows from the abstract.

study_context.population_setting: Systematic review of randomized studies involving general ICU populations, including patients with and without the ability to communicate.
study_context.design_sample: 59 included articles: 37 music interventions and 22 nonmusic sound interventions; only one study directly compared music with nonmusic sound.
study_context.intervention_exposure: Music and nonmusic sound interventions delivered in ICU settings; protocols varied across studies.
study_context.comparator: Standard care and/or noise-reduction controls depending on the included trial.
study_context.timing_duration: Intervention timing and duration varied across the randomized studies.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Pain, sleep, stress/anxiety, relaxation, cortisol, sedative/analgesic use, vital signs and haemodynamic measures.
study_context.results_detail: Both slow-tempo music and nonmusic sound interventions were associated in included trials with improvements in several outcomes including pain, sleep, stress/anxiety and relaxation. The review reported a larger evidence base for music than nonmusic sound for stress biomarkers, vital signs and haemodynamic measures.
study_context.study_limitations_context: The evidence base was much larger for music than nonmusic sound, and only one included study directly compared the two intervention categories.

study_design: Meta-analysis: 12 randomized trials, 1,301 participants across age groups
exposure: White noise for sleep; adult, older-adult and infant populations.
finding: Adult and older-adult pooled sleep-quality scores improved; adult results had substantial heterogeneity.
limitations: Infant findings cannot simply transfer to adult hospital cases. Sleep outcomes do not establish acute stress relief or an exact device volume.

study_context.population_setting: 12 randomized controlled trials with 1,301 participants: 356 infants/young children, 648 adults aged 18–64, and 297 adults aged ≥65. The review included critically ill and non-critically ill populations.
study_context.design_sample: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of white noise and sleep.
study_context.intervention_exposure: White-noise interventions; protocols and settings varied across trials.
study_context.comparator: Control conditions from the included RCTs, such as usual care or no white-noise intervention.
study_context.timing_duration: Exposure duration varied across studies; analyses were stratified by age group and clinical setting.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), total sleep time, sleep efficiency, number of awakenings and wake after sleep onset.
study_context.results_detail: In adults, pooled PSQI decreased by 3.70 points (95% CI -4.90 to -2.50; P<0.001); in older adults by 2.71 points (95% CI -4.98 to -0.44; P=0.02). PSQI also decreased in ICU patients (MD -4.04, 95% CI -6.35 to -1.73; P<0.001) and non-ICU settings (MD -2.61, 95% CI -3.84 to -1.38; P<0.001). Infant/young-child outcomes were mixed across total sleep time, sleep efficiency and awakenings.
study_context.study_limitations_context: Adult PSQI analyses showed substantial heterogeneity. Several subgroup outcomes contained few studies, limiting sensitivity analyses.

verified_from: Publisher abstract and study methods (corrected playback time)
study_design: Randomized trial: 58 ICU patients in Taiwan
exposure: 40–50 dB white noise from 23:00 to 06:00 for three consecutive nights versus routine care.
finding: Some self-reported sleep measures improved during follow-up.
limitations: Small single-setting trial; overnight sound is not equivalent to a 15-minute simulation. Volume percentage has no established conversion to decibels.

study_context.population_setting: 58 ICU patients in a medical center in southern Taiwan; 29 intervention and 29 control; mean age 61.7 ± 13.6 years; 56.9% male.
study_context.design_sample: Experimental longitudinal randomized controlled trial using block randomization, conducted March 2023 to August 2024.
study_context.intervention_exposure: White noise at 40–50 dB from 23:00 to 06:00 for three consecutive nights.
study_context.comparator: Routine ICU care without white noise.
study_context.timing_duration: Three consecutive overnight exposures; sleep was measured at baseline and on days 1, 3 and 5.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Verran and Snyder-Halpern Sleep Scale (VSHSS), including total sleep score, sleep disturbance, sleep effectiveness and sleep supplementation.
study_context.results_detail: Compared with control, the intervention group showed greater reductions in total sleep scores and sleep disturbances on days 1, 3 and 5 (P<0.01), improved sleep effectiveness on days 3 and 5 (P<0.01), and higher sleep supplementation on day 3 (P<0.01).
study_context.study_limitations_context: Single-center study with a small sample; outcomes were subjectively assessed using VSHSS.

exposure: Music and sound interventions across settings.
finding: Physiological and self-reported responses vary with preferences, delivery and cultural context; some adverse responses were reported.
limitations: Heterogeneous findings do not establish a universally beneficial or harmless sound.

study_context.population_setting: Scoping review of adult clinical and laboratory research on sound interventions and mental stress.
study_context.design_sample: 34 studies published from 1990–2024, including randomized controlled trials, clinical trials and laboratory experiments.
study_context.intervention_exposure: Music, natural sounds and speech, with variation in sound type, delivery method and listening context.
study_context.comparator: Comparators varied across studies and included control or alternative sound conditions.
study_context.timing_duration: Intervention timing and duration varied across the included studies.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Physiological markers such as HRV, cortisol and blood pressure, alongside self-reported stress and related outcomes.
study_context.results_detail: Music—especially classical and self-selected music—was frequently associated with reductions in physiological stress markers. Nonmusic sounds also showed potential effects, while responses varied with individual preferences and contextual factors; some included studies reported adverse responses.
study_context.study_limitations_context: The included studies were heterogeneous in setting, sound type, participant characteristics, delivery protocol and outcome measures.

study_design: Systematic review: 25 studies, all assessed at high risk of bias
exposure: Light exposure and vagally mediated HRV in healthy and clinical populations.
finding: Higher-illuminance blue light generally corresponded to lower vmHRV; lower-illuminance warm light showed potential increases, with inconsistent findings.
limitations: High risk of bias and heterogeneity prevent treating warm tone as proven calming or diagnosing state from HRV.

study_context.population_setting: Systematic review of healthy and clinical populations exposed to visible light of varying illuminance and color.
study_context.design_sample: 25 studies included after screening 24,673 records; all included studies were rated high risk of bias.
study_context.intervention_exposure: Ocular exposure to visible light varying in illuminance and color, including blue, red/warm and white-light conditions.
study_context.timing_duration: Exposure protocols and durations varied substantially across the literature.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Vagally mediated heart-rate variability (vmHRV) under different light-exposure conditions.
study_context.results_detail: Higher-illuminance blue light was generally associated with reduced vmHRV, while lower-illuminance warm-colored light such as red or dim white showed potential increases in vmHRV. Findings were inconsistent across studies.
study_context.study_limitations_context: All included studies were judged high risk of bias, with substantial heterogeneity in populations, exposure protocols and control conditions.

study_design: Systematic review: 28 ICU studies, 14 intervention studies
exposure: Naturalistic and intervention lighting research in intensive care.
finding: Marked heterogeneity prevented definitive outcome conclusions and clear lighting-design guidance.
limitations: ICU evidence cannot establish universal parameters or a guaranteed sleep benefit.

study_context.population_setting: Systematic review of ICU patient-lighting research published between 2015 and 2026.
study_context.design_sample: 12,674 records screened; 28 studies included. Fourteen evaluated lighting interventions and fourteen examined naturalistic ICU lighting conditions.
study_context.intervention_exposure: Interventions included dynamic lighting, static lighting, bright-light therapy and multicomponent lighting; observational studies assessed existing ICU lighting conditions.
study_context.comparator: Comparators varied by study, including standard lighting, alternative lighting conditions, or observational comparisons.
study_context.timing_duration: Lighting protocols and observation periods varied substantially across studies.
study_context.outcomes_measured: A range of patient health outcomes and lighting-condition measures across ICU studies.
study_context.results_detail: Some studies reported potential benefits of specific lighting interventions, but findings were inconsistent and no definitive pattern emerged across the heterogeneous outcome and lighting measures.
study_context.study_limitations_context: Marked heterogeneity in interventions, lighting measurement, health outcomes and study methods; reporting of lighting conditions was inconsistent.

study_design: Systematic review of electrodermal measurement and processing
exposure: Tonic and phasic electrodermal activity and applications.
finding: EDA reflects sympathetic sweat-gland activity and is used across multiple arousal-related applications.
limitations: EDA alone is not a specific psychological stress diagnosis. The AHR absolute-only reporting rule is a prototype convention.

study_context.population_setting: Systematic review of electrodermal activity (EDA) measurement, signal processing and applications across psychophysiological and pathophysiological research.
study_context.design_sample: Methodological/systematic review rather than a single intervention cohort.
study_context.intervention_exposure: No single intervention; the review covers tonic and phasic EDA acquisition and processing methods.
study_context.timing_duration: Measurement windows and processing approaches varied across the literature reviewed.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Tonic skin-conductance level, phasic skin-conductance responses, acquisition methods and signal-processing approaches.
study_context.results_detail: EDA reflects sympathetic innervation of sweat glands. The review describes use of EDA in emotional/cognitive stress research and applications including fatigue, pain, sleepiness, exercise recovery, epilepsy, neuropathies and depression.
study_context.study_limitations_context: EDA is used across diverse applications and processing methods; the review emphasizes measurement and processing methodology rather than a single disease- or intervention-specific effect.

verified_from: Publisher abstract, eligibility and selected intervention-table sections
study_design: Review: 13 studies, 1,975 hospitalized adults and older adults; noncritical wards
exposure: Nursing interventions including environmental, sensory, educational and individualized care.
finding: Reported sleep-focused approaches span multiple components, including light and noise management.
limitations: Critical-care patients were excluded; multicomponent evidence cannot establish an isolated light/sound effect or AHR dose.

study_context.population_setting: Systematic review of hospitalized adults and older adults in noncritical hospital wards.
study_context.design_sample: 712 records identified; 13 studies included with 1,975 participants; findings synthesized narratively.
study_context.intervention_exposure: Sleep-promoting nursing interventions spanning educational/communication strategies, dietary and sensory interventions, symptom and environmental control, daily activity planning, sleep assessment/documentation and individualized nursing care.
study_context.comparator: Comparator conditions varied across the included studies.
study_context.timing_duration: Intervention schedules and follow-up varied across studies.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Sleep-related outcomes and implementation of nursing interventions intended to promote sleep.
study_context.results_detail: The review identified multiple recurring categories of nursing sleep interventions, including environmental and sensory approaches, and emphasized a multidimensional approach incorporating physical, psychosocial and relational aspects of care.
study_context.study_limitations_context: Critical-care patients were not the target population; the included interventions and outcome measures were heterogeneous.

exposure: Nurse-led SLEEP bundle including noise/light reduction, sensory aids and pharmacological/nonpharmacological measures.
finding: Reported sleep questionnaire scores rose from 62 to 70 after implementation.
limitations: Bundle and before/after design do not isolate lighting or sound causality. Medication components are outside AHR.

study_context.population_setting: Quality-improvement study in a 12-bed surgical ICU in Wuhan, China.
study_context.design_sample: Quasi-experimental before/after evidence-based quality-improvement programme using the Framework of Evidence-based Continuous Quality Improvement and the Ottawa Model of Research Use.
study_context.intervention_exposure: Nurse-led SLEEP Bundle: Sleep initiative; Light control; Eye mask/earplugs; Environment noise cancellation; and Provision of non-pharmacological support (including aromatherapy/music) and pharmacological support (including dexmedetomidine/painkillers).
study_context.comparator: Pre-implementation ICU care versus post-implementation care.
study_context.timing_duration: Programme-level implementation with before/after assessment; the abstract does not isolate a single environmental exposure duration.
study_context.outcomes_measured: Patient-perceived sleep quality using the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire, nurses' knowledge/attitudes/actions and adherence to sleep-promotion practices.
study_context.results_detail: Median Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire score increased from 62 (IQR 48–72) to 70 (IQR 62–76), with P<0.001. Nurse knowledge/action measures and adherence to several sleep-management practices also improved after implementation.
study_context.study_limitations_context: Multicomponent before/after quality-improvement design; the programme combined environmental, sensory, educational, non-pharmacological and pharmacological components.

verified_from: PubMed / Journal of the Acoustical Society of America record
study_design: Hospital-wide acoustic survey at Johns Hopkins Hospital
exposure: Equivalent continuous sound pressure levels measured by location, frequency and time of day across Johns Hopkins Hospital.
finding: Average equivalent sound levels were generally in the 50–60 dB(A) range, and many units showed little or no nighttime reduction in noise.
limitations: Observational environmental measurement study; it does not test patient outcomes or show that any AHR sound choice improves sleep or recovery.

verified_from: Verified AHR literature workbook + publication record
study_design: Systematic literature review of wearable-device stress monitoring
exposure: Wearable HR, HRV, EDA and related signals used in stress-monitoring research.
finding: HRV, heart rate and EDA are commonly used contextual biomarkers, but datasets and methods vary and generalization across people/settings remains difficult.
limitations: Many datasets are small or short and biomarker validity/generalization are limited; does not justify diagnosing stress from one signal or threshold.

study_design: Secondary analysis of preferred music selected by mechanically ventilated ICU patients enrolled in a randomized trial; N=126
exposure: Patient-selected music used within a music-listening intervention.
finding: Patients selected a wide range of music, reinforcing that clinically used music should be individualized rather than assumed to be universally calming.
limitations: Preference analysis does not establish that music is superior to silence or another sound for a given patient, and the population was mechanically ventilated ICU patients.

study_design: Systematic review; 15 studies (2012–2026), N=2,024 hospitalized patients, mostly intensive care
exposure: Calming music, nature sounds and white noise delivered from brief sessions to continuous overnight exposure.
finding: Sound-based interventions were associated overall with improved sleep quality, but effect sizes varied and several studies found no significant benefit.
limitations: Substantial heterogeneity in sound type, setting, timing, duration and outcome measurement; does not establish a universal best sound or AHR volume/duration.

study_design: Peer-reviewed CHI qualitative study; semi-structured interviews with 20 rehabilitation-hospital patients
exposure: Smart patient rooms with digitally controllable entertainment and environment using touchscreen, voice and accessibility controls.
finding: Patients described smart-room technology as potentially transformative for people with reduced motor function by supporting independence and control over their surroundings; the study also identified implementation challenges and staff-support needs.
limitations: Single rehabilitation hospital and qualitative interviews; does not test automated physiological adaptation, clinical outcomes, or a specific light/sound intervention.

study_design: Peer-reviewed CHI qualitative study; 23 hospital employees across nine occupational groups
exposure: Real smart patient rooms with controllable lights, blinds, thermostat, TV and soundbar in a rehabilitation hospital.
finding: Employees reported benefits and drawbacks of smart-room controls; the work highlights that patients and staff can have different needs and suggests configurable limits such as light brightness or maximum audio volume to avoid overstimulation while preserving use.
limitations: Single rehabilitation hospital; qualitative study; does not validate AHR thresholds, automated recommendations, clinical efficacy or a particular environmental action.
